transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-31
Start: 16:32 PDT
Duration: ~46 min
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Gonzalez (Sunrise Lead Eng), James Lee (Sunrise CTO), Arun Sharma (Sunrise PM)

Auto Summary (auto-gen): Quick hosted chat intro and handoff; focus on streaming parameters and retry/fallback playbook.

[00:00] Alex Kim: hey everyone, thanks for joining, can you hear me okay?
[00:05] Maya Gonzalez: yeah, loud and clear, thanks Alex. we have a mix of engineering and product — we'll mostly watch the demo and ask questions about reliability and cost.
[00:12] James Lee: quick note, main success metric is sub-200ms tail p95 on short assistant replies for the triage flow, and keep token cost below our current baseline — so we need concrete numbers.
[00:22] Alex Kim: totally, we'll walk through the hosted chat API, how streaming works, which params change latency vs token output, and our retry/backoff and fallback patterns. Priya will run a short console demo after the API bits.
[00:30] Priya Patel: hi — i'll jump into the sandbox and show a quick convo with streaming so you can see partial tokens as they arrive.

[02:05] Speaker 1: (background) small delay on my side but catching up.
[03:00] Alex Kim: ok first concept: streaming vs sync responses. streaming sends incremental chunks — lower time-to-first-byte for the user but you need to handle partial events and resume logic on client-side for reconnects. we recommend a 2-5s client-side idle timeout and then retry with an idempotency token.
[03:45] Maya Gonzalez: when you say idempotency token, is that at request-level? what happens if we retry and the model continues streaming new tokens?
[03:53] Alex Kim: good question — our hosted API supports an idempotency_key header. if you retry with the same key within the window (default 60s) we attempt to return the same completion, or if the original succeeded we return the final result. if the request partially completed and the connection dropped, a reconnect with the same key will stream remaining tokens or return cached final payload depending on timing and prefix cache — there's some heuristics.
[04:20] Arun Sharma: that prefix cache — is that KV cache? can you force a cold run?
[04:26] Priya Patel: we use a few layers: prefix/KV caching at the runtime and ongoing request-level caching. for deterministic testing you can set disable_cache=true in the call, but for production we usually keep cache enabled to save cost and reduce latency. note: booleans and param names in SDK might differ (we have examples in the docs).
[05:10] James Lee: and how do you handle duplicate tokens on retry? like if client timed out and replayed?
[05:18] Alex Kim: we tag streaming events with offsets and a final "done" event. clients should dedupe by offset. we also recommend idempotent rewrite on your websocket client — simple approach is to accept tokens until the same offset seen, then ignore duplicates.
[06:00] Priya Patel: demo time — sandbox console. sharing my screen. (screen share noise)
[06:12] Priya Patel: opening example chat, prompt set is a triage flow. hitting generate with streaming mode on. you'll see chunks pop in.
[07:05] [console stream] partial: "Sure — can you tell me the patient's main symptom?"
[07:22] Maya Gonzalez: nice, so that's delta streaming. what's the per-chunk size?
[07:28] Priya Patel: chunking is internal — we emit token deltas roughly every 50-150ms depending on model and batch load. you can control 'stream_interval' at a coarse level but most teams use default.
[08:10] Alex Kim: back to params — the big levers: temperature/top_p for diversity, max_tokens and stop sequences for length control, and frequency_penalty/presence_penalty where applicable. on hosted, using lower temperature reduces unexpected tails and often lowers token usage because responses are more concise.
[08:45] Arun Sharma: if we want determinism for legal copy, do you have a deterministic mode?
[08:52] Priya Patel: not strictly deterministic but you can pin model version and set low temperature + beam-like sampling via top_p=0.0 (or 0.01) — gives much more repeatable outputs; we also recommend using eval harness to assert invariants.
[09:30] James Lee: ok cost — what's typical token cost if we run typical triage prompt?
[09:36] Alex Kim: depends on model, but hosted default model for this demo is redwood-1-small-ish (we showed curated models in the catalog). ballpark: 0.0006$/1k tokens for base tier — we'll send exact pricing. the big cost is output tokens; using stop sequences and controlling max_tokens helps. Also prefix caching helps for repeated prompts.
[10:10] Maya Gonzalez: switching gears — retries. what do we recommend for client backoff?
[10:16] Alex Kim: exponential backoff with jitter is standard. for streaming we suggest 500ms -> 1s -> 2s -> abort by 10s total unless you have a hard requirement to keep trying. for short transient network blips we also support automatic server-side continuation if retry arrives with same idempotency key within 60s.
[10:45] Priya Patel: note on throttling: if you hit rate limits we return 429 with Retry-After; you should respect that and backoff. console has per-key metrics so you can tune concurrency.
[11:30] Maya Gonzalez: our traffic profile can spike during peak clinic hours — how do you recommend scaling in hosted?
[11:37] Alex Kim: hosted auto-scaling handles burst, but to guarantee p95 you can add a short warm-up and use reserved burst capacity on Dedicated; since this is hosted demo, auto-scaling should cover your initial pilot. we'll include guidance in the ops playbook.
[12:05] James Lee: do you offer per-route quotas? we'd like to isolate triage vs knowledge assistant.
[12:12] Priya Patel: yes per-route and per-token quotas; you can also tag API keys and use Console to surface per-route latency and cost.
[13:00] [15:00] Speaker 2: (crosstalk)
[14:50] Alex Kim: quick safety note — hosted comes with content filters and response policies, you can opt-in or apply client-side checks. for health use-cases you probably want a review layer.
[15:30] Priya Patel: demo — now showing failure mode. i'm going to simulate a socket drop and show reconnect with the same idempotency key.
[15:40] [console stream] partial tokens... connection lost... reconnecting...
[16:05] Priya Patel: reconnect sent with same key, console shows server returned cached completion and resumed streaming final event — you can see client dedupe needed.
[16:30] Maya Gonzalez: nice. what about partial credits? if the response stopped halfway do we get charged?
[16:36] Alex Kim: we charge for tokens generated by the model; if the model completed and you didn't receive it due to client issue but the server generated tokens, you'd still be billed. there's cost controls though — set max_tokens and stop sequences to reduce unexpected long outputs.
[17:10] James Lee: can you throttle or limit per-user?
[17:14] Priya Patel: yes, token-based quotas and rate-limits per API key and per-user identifier in our rate rules.
[18:00] Alex Kim: let's go over recommended client pattern: 1) use streaming for snappy UI, 2) attach an idempotency_key per user-request, 3) dedupe by offset on replays, 4) exponential backoff with jitter, 5) set conservative max_tokens and stop sequences.
[18:45] Arun Sharma: about model fallbacks — if the primary model is busy or you're throttling, can you failover to a cheaper/lower-latency model?
[18:52] Priya Patel: yes, smart routing supports fallback model variants. you can configure policy: latency-first, cost-first, or strict pinned. fallback preserves the same API shape, but outputs may vary; we recommend A/B test on a small percentage first.
[19:30] Maya Gonzalez: what's the expected difference in latency between models?
[19:35] Alex Kim: smaller models give much faster token times — e.g., p50 could go from 60ms to 20ms per token depending on sequence length and batching. again we'll run benchmark with your prompts.
[20:05] James Lee: can we run a short live benchmark now? maybe one or two sample prompts?
[20:12] Maya Gonzalez: we prepared two sample prompts — short triage and longer note summarization.
[20:20] Priya Patel: ok let's run the short triage first. sending request to hosted-gen with streaming on and idempotency_key set.
[21:00] [console] streamed partial answer in 140ms first chunk, final in 420ms — p50 first-byte 140ms, p95 ~ 520ms in this run.
[21:30] Maya Gonzalez: that's promising. can you capture the logs and token counts?
[21:35] Priya Patel: yes I'll attach the run to the benchmark spreadsheet and include token breakdown.
[22:00] Alex Kim: quick question from SE best practices — for the note summarization long prompt, consider truncating with smart windowing to avoid large input tokens; also use streaming so UI shows progress.
[23:10] James Lee: regulatory & data residency — we're in healthcare, do you offer audit logs and SOC 2?
[23:18] Alex Kim: yes hosted has SOC 2 compliance, audit logs, and customer-level retention controls. for stricter residency we offer Private (VPC) deployments — but that adds ops overhead and licensing. We'll share security pack (SOC2, ISO, pentest).
[24:00] Maya Gonzalez: great — please send those docs.
[24:10] Alex Kim: will do.
[24:30] Arun Sharma: one more on retries — how do we avoid double billing if we accidentally replay?
[24:38] Priya Patel: idempotency and server-side dedupe reduce this risk; if you replay with same key we detect prior successful completions and return cached results. partial plays where model generated tokens but didn't mark done are tricky — we still bill for tokens generated. the safe approach is shorter max_tokens and smaller stops.
[25:20] Alex Kim: ok time for a quick console tour of the Optimize tab — shows token breakdown per-route, sample latency histograms, and suggestion engine for batching and quantization (quantization applies more to Dedicated/Private).
[26:05] Priya Patel: here's an example suggestion: reduce batch size and enable prefix caching for 10% lower token spend on repeated prompts. we also surface when model drift increases and recommend re-eval.
[27:00] Maya Gonzalez: that suggestion engine — do you run it automatically on our traffic or is it manual?
[27:06] Priya Patel: Console's Optimize runs passive analysis on route traces and provides recommendations; applying them requires a config change. we can also run a manual consult as an add-on.
[28:10] James Lee: ok what's the pilot setup? we'd want a 2-week pilot with 100k tokens/day cap and SLA for latency test.
[28:18] Alex Kim: we can do that — pilot terms are usually flexible. I'll propose a pilot commitment and include an escape clause if latency misses SLOs.
[29:00] Maya Gonzalez: last question: how do you handle tokenization differences? our current metrics use a different tokenizer token counts.
[29:08] Priya Patel: we provide tokenization tool in SDK so you can compute exact token counts pre-call; also Console token_count reports are model-specific. we'll share a script to align your metrics.
[30:00] [wrap up] Alex Kim: recap: Alex send pricing & SLA + security pack; Priya run latency/token benchmark; Maya share sample prompts and traffic profile. target dates in next_steps.
[30:30] James Lee: sounds good. thanks for the demo.
[30:35] Maya Gonzalez: thanks — we'll review and get the samples to you.
[30:40] Alex Kim: one more note — i'll include a short ops playbook with recommended client retry pseudocode and sample SDK snippets for idempotency.
[31:00] Arun Sharma: perfect.
[31:10] Priya Patel: ok closing recording. thanks all.

(Transcript end — minor speaker mislabels possible, some short gaps removed.)
